title: What Have You Been Watching? (Week of (December 24, 2023)

commenti.body: Last night I saw *Dinah East* — the full 1970 movie, not the short edited version. Incredibly low-budget yet very avant-garde for its time, it's the tale of a Hollywood star who is discovered, only after her sudden death, to have been not a woman (as everyone had thought, for years and years) but a man. The plot mainly consists of flashbacks involving Dinah's kind acts toward others while struggling to keep the big secret and seeking love. Warhol star Ultra Violet plays an important role. It's really an interesting watch, with real insights about trust, integrity and what connects us.

**Sicario** directed by Denis Villeneuve (USA, 2015) - An intense (and at times rather nasty) story from the endless 'war on drugs' along the USA/ Mexico border.  Visually astonishing and tautly edited, with impressive performances by Emily Blunt (as a clueless FBI agent) and Benicio del Toro (as a freelance killer).  Not for the faint of heart.

**My Blueberry Nights** (2007) directed by Wong Kar-wai - A confection more than a film, its a road movie about loneliness and loss set in New York City & Memphis & Las Vegas.  Didn't do well with either critics or audiences, perhaps because of its strange, sluggish pace.  I enjoyed watching it and have fallen in love with Nora Jones.

**Fallen Angels** directed by Wong Kar-wai (Hong Kong, 1995) - A visual feast of a film, although I found its frenetic editing rather tiring (it seems a much longer movie than its runtime: 96 minutes).  Same themes and style as this director's earlier, and superior, **Chungking Express** (1994), but the mute, anarchistic character of Ho Chi-mo sours this film.  Music is thoughtfully chosen throughout, but I especially liked the strange song *Only You* by the Flying Pickets which closes the film.

HEAT (1995) - Michael Mann: The greatest film of 1995, the greatest film Michael Mann ever made, and also one of the great films of all time.

NO COUNTRY FOR OLD MEN (2007) - Coen Bros. - Aside from the Lord of the Rings movies, this may be my favorite film of the 21st century to date. Or at least in my top 5. And there’s a little bit of humor here but in a much drier vein. The relentless and somber poetry of this movie is classic.

THE RAPTURE (1991) - Messy, sometimes quite overt, and has its flaws. But ultimately gripping, haunting, serious. A masterwork. Underrated. Deserves the Criterion treatment.

A CHARLIE BROWN CHRISTMAS/HOW THE GRINCH STOLE CHRISTMAS: Classic cartoon Christmas creations. Even if you’ve seen them more than once, or their successors, the originals always stay fresh somehow. Somehow Christmas has a way of catching up to the resistant spirit (some).

LA CONFIDENTIAL (1997): One of my favorite films of all time. Everything about this is near-perfect, and it’s one of the best of a kind of “neo-classic” movie that makes you feel like you’re watching an old-school classic from the Golden Age days but with a fresh, modern, more overt energy (like BRAVEHEART, GOLDENEYE, MASK OF ZORRO, or PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN: CURSE OF THE BLACK PEARL). Its most obvious companion contrast is CHINATOWN, which is more the serious Great Movie with capital letters. But this is a masterpiece in a slightly more “humble” but no less awesome way.

I looooooove The Rapture and have seen it a bunch of times - so shocking, so moving. Some parts clearly could have had a bigger budget but the premise and actors and script are amazing. Mark Kermode recently cited it when talking about Knock At The Cabin as a superior movie that shared an idea of 'what if these religious beliefs were literally true?'

[Metropia 2009](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/metropia/) Is a very different type of dystopian sci-fi, with unique animation based on photorealistic faces made strange. It's fair enough, a fairly standard dystopian loner adventure in the manner of The Matrix. 3.5/5

[Boy and Bicycle 1965](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/boy-and-bicycle-1965/) Ridley Scott's first film, a short made with his brother Tony as a boy hwo plays hooky from school to meditate on life at the beach. Made with a microbudget, shows great promise, I'm sure he'll be the next Alain Resnais. 3.5/5

[Kin-dza-dza 1986](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/kin-dza-dza/) I'm on a campaign to make more people aware of this weird and very fun Soviet sci-fi adventure, kind of like the Wizard of Oz meets Mad Max. Free to watch on Mosfilm's great YouTube channel [HERE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AUtZOl_QxvY). A blast. 4/5

[Butterfly 1999](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/butterfly-1999/) To my mind, pairs with Amarcord as the story of a young boy growing up in a small town in the 30s, and the rise of fascism. Not as exuberant as Amarcord, in fact very conventional historical coming-of-age drama, but very well made. 4/5

CHRISTMAS 1 [Kiss Kiss Bang Bang 2005](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/kiss-kiss-bang-bang-2005/) Shane Black goes full meta in a story packed with one liners and a deeply disturbing and grim storyline. Maybe this is a bit too much Shane for one film. 3.5/5

CHRISTMAS 2 [The Long Kiss Goodnight 1996](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/the-long-kiss-goodnight/) This is how you do a Christmas action thriller comedy. Action top notch, characterisation superb, dialogue witty and entertaining. All the Shane tropes are present including "I'm too old for this shit". 4/5

CHRISTMAS 3 [American Psycho 2000](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/american-psycho/) The blackest of black comedies is a treat all the way through. Ambivalent action paired with satirical intent, it's the most end-of-Millenium experience you could have bar Fight Club. 4.5/5

CHRISTMAS 4 Eyes Wide Shut 1999 The most heartwarming of Christmas movies, my family like to curl up on Christmas Day to watch this, and figure out what's up with the secret society that Kubrick doesn't want to show us? 5/5

Guy Ritchie's The Covenant

Probably reviewed here a bunch of times but in my opinion really worth a mention when we discuss the best movies of this year. The structure and message of the movie is pretty clear and simple but that doesn't diminish the fact that the story is being told in well-executed fashion, accompanied by great cinematography, intense action scenes and a potent soundtrack. This is quite different from Guy Ritchie's usual style but in this case that's not a bad thing at all. He offers Jake Gyllenhaal and Dar Salim plenty of opportunities to show some great acting. 

Solid 8/10 (maybe 0.5 bonus points for using a song for the end credits that every Breaking Bad lover knows).

The “villain” Long Kiss Goodnight ruins it. He doesn’t ruin the whole picture. But his past experience was as a theatre actor and boy does it show. You can tell he’s a chorus boy. Everyone else is banging it out, and here’s a guy from A Chorus Line as the villain. Awful casting decision.

And you gather the family around to watch Eyes Wide Shut? A film with secret sex parties and a girl who skips town after contracting hiv? This Christmas introduce them to Requiem for a Dream, and Oldboy. Or Whore.
Heat is great but I think Collateral is better. I mean how often do we get to see Cruise play the baddest villain in town?

I watched a few Triad films: Election, Election 2, Young and Dangerous.

Young and Dangerous seems to idealize the lifestyle a bit more than the others, but I loved the atmosphere. A lot of handheld shots of Hong Kong streets which gives the film a strong sense of place.

Election on the other hand is more grounded and challenges the notions of criminal loyalty and brotherhood. The whole movie is about gangsters scheming to fulfill their own selfish ambitions as two men attempt to be crowned as leader of the underworld.

I particularly loved the subplot of Election where various underlings are sent to collect a McGuffin-type Baton that’s imbued with significance because it’s an item traditionally held in the care of the organization’s leader. So there’s this overarching plot of strategic maneuvering while characters also allocate resources to collecting a trump card, giving the film a ticking clock element.

Sure, we're all degenerates in my house. I believe strongly in the importance of cultivating deviance in young people. 

I like your suggestions but everyone knows Requiem for a Dream is for Easter, Oldboy is for Korean New Year, and Whore is for Valentine's Day.

I feel like I’m a long lost relative of yours. Polyester is for Yom Kippur. Serial Mom is Hanukkah. A Serbian Film for Rosh Hashanah. John Waters and Divine really instilled in people that filth is good.

Did a re-watch of **Satyajit Ray’s Apu Trilogy** this week:

**Pather Panchali (1955, Satyajit Ray) — re-watch** — I liked this one a lot more on re-watch than I did the first time. I think its slow-burn pace is a lot easier to appreciate after having already seen the rest of the trilogy once — it feels sort of like revisiting memories of an old childhood friend. Although Satyajit Ray captures the hardships of life in poverty well, his primary aim in this film is less to make us sympathize with the Bengali poor and more to make us empathize with them, recognizing their humanity in full complexity. He does it beautifully. **10/10**

**Aparajito (1956, Satyajit Ray) — re-watch** — While I remember *Pather* being my least favourite the first time I watched through the trilogy, *Aparajito* struck me as being the weakest one on re-watch. While none of the films in the trilogy have plots in the conventional sense, this one feels the most disjointed, and you can kind of feel that it was a mixture of elements from what were originally two different stories. And while I’m not going to give spoilers, I thought the way they mixed it made the parallels between the ending to this one and that of the first movie seem a little too heavy-handed. I’m being really nit-picky here, though. Even the weakest of these movies is still a must-see. **9/10**

**The World of Apu (1959, Satyajit Ray) — re-watch** — Previously I regarded this as by far the best of the Apu films. I think I’d now put this second behind *Pather*, but that’s purely due to how much *Pather* went up in my estimation; this film is just as touching as it ever was. A worthy conclusion to one of the all-time great film trilogies. **10/10**

Because I had a long flight again this week, I also ended up watching **Phineas and Ferb the Movie: Candace Against the Universe (2020, Bob Bowen)** and **Despicable Me (2010, Chris Renaud/Pierre Coffin)**, the second one being a re-watch. Both were **6/10**s.

**Movie of the week**: *Pather Panchali*

***Week # 155 (Year 3/Week 51):***

My first Singaporean film, Anthony Chen's award-winning debut feature, **Ilo Ilo** (2013). There is a new sub-genre emerging in recent years, realistic dramas about live-in maids and domestic workers (Many from South America and from South-East Asia: 'Lina from Lima', 'The second mother', 'La Nana', 'Roma', 'La cieniga', 'A simple life', and also others I haven't seen). Most are terrific, and so is this one, with 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes.

\[That [Wikipedia list of movies with 100% score on RT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_100%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes) is often a reliable indicator for the type of fair I like to spend my time with\]. **Highly recommended – 9/10.**

🍿

**2 more by Aki Kaurismäki:**

🍿 My 10th tragic feature by him, and possibly my favorite, **The match factory girl** (1990). The great Kati Outinen is a sad and lonely young woman who has a one-night stand. Minimalist, bleak and unrelenting, this was no Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale. Considered by some as the "Best Finnish film". **9/10.**

🍿 **To Each His Own Cinema**, a 2007 anthology of 34 3-minute shorts by different directors about how movies inspired them. Takeshii Kitano, the Dardenne brothers, Zhang Zimou, Jane Campion, Atom Egoyan, Gus Van Sant, Lars von Trier, Roman Polanski, Michael Cimino, David Cronenberg, Wong Kar-wai, Ken Loach, Claude Lelouche, David Lynch, Etc. It was commissioned to celebrate 60th anniversary of The Cannes Film Festival.

The often-repetitive stories were about old cinema houses out in the country, ticket taking, projectionists, watching Bresson and Fellini in small villages, and similar wet dreams for cineastes. A nice touch was that the credits were shown only at the end of each short, so you could try to guess who directed it while watching.

Most of the films were not very good. Among the few stand outs were Hou Hsiao-hsien (A family in 1940s Taiwan goes to see a film in a suddenly decrepit theater), Aki Kaurismäki (Foundry workers on lunch break enjoy a Lumiére silent film of workers on lunch break), Abbas Kiarostami (Iranian women watch 'Romeo and Juliet' and cry), Wim Wenders (The inhabitants of a remote Congo village watch Black Hawk Down) and The Coen Brothers ([A cowboy resembling Llewellyn Moss at a repertory art house, debating if he should see Renoir or Nuri Bilge Ceylon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y4AeXMEIeNI)).

🍿

Ridley Scott's first stream-of-consciousness film, **Boy and Bicycle**. Made in 1962, when he was 23, and starring his 16 year old brother, Tony \[who would jump to his death from the San Pedro Bridge exactly 50 years later\]. A boy skips school, and wanders round the empty docks of his West Hartlepool industrial seaside town. Like a working class scene from 'Dubliners'.

It took Ridley 15 years before he was able to direct his next movie, during which time he specialized in producing commercial advertising. His most famous one, **The bike Ride**, [an advert for bread](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NkonymPyp5g), also featured a boy on a bike. It was later voted as the 'Best British Advert of all time'.

🍿

**My 7th and 8th films by Sofia Coppola:**

🍿 **Priscilla**, another pretty young woman living in a privileged gilded cage (like Coppola's herself did). A beautiful romance without sex, and with an oppressive power imbalance. "The Elvis" and the 14 year old girl \[and without a single Elvis song\]. 7/10.

🍿 In her shallow **The Bling Ring** (2013), a group of celebrities-wannabes Valley Girls burgles from Hollywood celebrities homes, and become mini-celebrities themselves. It was pretty, but I couldn't find any deeper meaning there.

🍿

Danish cinema produced dozens of 'Danish Noir' works in the 1940's, during the Nazi occupation, and the 1950's. **Mordets melodi ("Melody of murder"**, 1944) is considered Denmark's first horror film, and is my first movie directed by the great Bodil Ipsen. \[The Danish "Oscars" are actually called "The Bodil's" after her and the other female influencer, Bodil Kjer\].

Like Fritz Lang's 'M', a crazed, ambi-sexual killer continues to strangle women while singing a luring French cabaret song, and the dark, dramatic sets are visually stark.

🍿

Bradley Cooper's new adulatory bio-pic **Maestro**, about the larger-than-life, overbearing genius that was Leonard Bernstein. Uncanny recreation of his life, but mostly his bisexuality vs. his love for his wife and family. Carey Mulligan was tremendous in it. [So was Gustav Mahler](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bj6KLv7kv2Q). This is the year of the “Great Man” in movies, Napoleon, Oppenheimer, Ferrari, Bernstein…

🍿

**First-watch earlier Buñuel X 2:**

🍿 **Nazarin** (1959), Buñuel‘s own favorite work, about a saintly priest, who mistakenly tries to follow in Christ's footsteps. But all his literal interpretations of the dogmas are proven to lead him, as well as his small coterie of freaks and miscasts, into misfortunes. One of the last of his Mexican films, this religious parable is the one that convinced the Spanish censors to allow him to return from exile.

🍿 Bunuel's only documentary (pseudo-documentary rather), **Land Without Bread** (1932), describing (exaggerated) misery in a remote Spanish town. Extreme poverty, hunger and destitute rarely seen on film.

🍿

**Dil Dhadakne Do** (2015) is an Indian soap opera, staged on a first-class Turkish cruise ship in the Mediterranean, directed by a woman, and narrated by a dog. It's a 3-hour long American-style 'Rich and famous' sit-com of a large family, full of expected love intrigues of bland characters.

I was hoping for another hopping Song and Dance story, but there were only 3 dance numbers in it, [Gallan Goodiyaan](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jCEdTq3j-0U), Girls like to dance and the final credit scene.

🍿

**3 atypical Christmas fairy tales:**

🍿 My second unusual anime by Satoshi Kon, **Tokyo Godfathers** (2003, after 'Paprika'). An imaginative Christmas Miracle parable of The Three Magis. Except that here they are three unlikely homeless heroes, an alcoholic, a trans woman, and a teenage runaway who likes to spit on people from above. They discover an abandoned newborn while searching through the garbage for presents. Emotional and unorthodox. **8/10.**

🍿 **The Bloody Olives** (1997), a Belgian meta Film Noir of a husband, his wife and her lover who keep murdering each other again and again while decorating their Christmas tree. Full of twists and double crosses.

🍿 *"One morning, as Gregor Samsa woke from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a giant banana..."*

Malcolm Tucker's Oscar-winning parody **Franz Kafka's It's a Wonderful Life** (1993) was not too convincing: It's too easy to parody Kranz Fuckfuck.

🍿

First watch: Truffaut's second installment of the Antoine Doinel's saga, **Antoine and Colette** (1962). The boy of '400 Blows' is now 17, and awkwardly falls in love for the first time. Youthfully charming.

🍿

*(Continued below...)*

*(Continued...)*

**2 by Norwegian Kristoffer Borgli:**

🍿 The first half of **Dream scenario** had me in stitches: Such an original thought experiment, and so unhesitatingly fresh. But exactly at mid-point, when everybody's dreams turn into nightmares, the story progressed into a underwhelming flirtation with broader contemporary themes, fame, cancel culture, public perception. The only anchor left in Paul's life is memories of his lovely wife, Julianne Nicholson. 6/10.

🍿 Checking out his only previous feature, **Sick of Myself**: That too was a story with an intriguing premise that opened very strong, end completely fizzled halfway. A young barista lives anonymously and unnoticed, being ignored by her self-centered boyfriend and acquaintances. One day at work, a woman is being mauled by a dog and she's the only one jumping to help her. While covered in blood, she is suddenly the center of attention. The rush causes her to start an insane dive into self-mutilation. The second half centered on narcissism, influencers, victimhood and social media, and was highly disappointing. My 5th film with Anders Danielsen Lie. 4/10.

🍿

*"Chip, you know how I hate the brown word"...*

My first black comedy from John Waters' commercial period, **Serial mom** (1994).

With Waters regulars Chesty Morgan, Tracy Lords, Mink Stole, Patty Hearst and Ricky Lake \[But it could do better with less Fat jokes\]. Also, with a lawyer named Nazelrod and a panties-sniffer named Marvin Pickles. The hot rock and roll girl band is called Camel Lips. So the anti-establishment humour is very elementary.

🍿

*“I Didn’t Come To Rescue Rambo From You. I Came Here To Rescue You From Him”…*

First watch: I did not expect **Rambo: first blood** (1982) to be that watchable, with such excellent Jerry Goldsmith score. A traumatized Vietnam vet feels spat on and maligned. And all the years I thought it but a thoughtless, jingoistic violent flick.

🍿

**3 more stand-ups:**

🍿 **Trevor Noah: Where Was I**, his latest stand-up opens with his best line upfront: "I really enjoy every day in America right now. The same way you'd enjoy your last day on earth". It has a few other good jokes, but otherwise it's pretty tame. The venue, The Fox Theater in Detroit, looks magnificent. 4/10

🍿 **Sane man**, my first stand-up with heavy-smoker, politically incorrect Bill Hicks. I heard the name before, but never seen him perform.

🍿 So, for the second time in a week, I re-watched **Dave Gorman’s Googlewhack Adventure**, a [contagiously funny presentation.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6eOfRvuWIxk)

🍿

**4 Shorts:**

🍿 Agnès Varda's **Les Fiancés du pont Mac Donald,** a Harold Lloyd and Buster Keaton-inspired silent comedy from 1962. With JL Godard and Anna Karina.

🍿 Re-watch: From David Firth's, the creator of 'Salad Fingers', the unsettling **Cream**. [Inventing a single solution to all of the world's problems.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0UgiJPnwtQU)

The credit page at the end is just as hilariously expansive as the bitter story itself.

🍿 **Figs,** a gentle 81-year-old black woman who survived a life of oppression, from the cotton fields of Louisiana to becoming a teacher in South Los Angeles.

🍿 **The girl with the yellow stockings,** a light German story of a young man asking his girlfriend to marry him again and again.

🍿

One I couldn't finish even after trying hard for nearly 20 minutes: The toothless, 1990's Clintonite-lite, political romance **Speechless.** Trying to cash in on the then real-life hookup between James Carville and Mary Matalin, it was awful on every level.

🍿

Finally watched *Judgment at Nuremberg*. Exceeded my already high expectations.

The movie felt sincere in its investigation into the problem at hand, which is surprising to see in an American movie regarding the WWII. I don't typically highlight the acting as an outstanding point of a movie, but this was something different. And I loved how they handled the interpretation problem.

**Shin Godzilla - 9/10**

Watched in preparation for Godzilla Minus One, and honestly if Minus One is even close to being as good as Shin I will enjoy it because I thought this was absolutely brilliant. Godzilla is finally back to being a huge allegorical horror, and this film totally masters the balancing act of human drama and the eponymous monster at the heart of it. Hollywood has so much to learn when it comes to this franchise, namely that it isn't the spectacle of Godzilla that is the most interesting, but rather what his arrival does to the characters around him. 

​

**The Killers of the Flower Moon - 10/10**

Far and away the best film of the year. Marty takes aim at American corruption once more, this time focusing on America's original sin - the genocide of indigenous populations. Lily Gladstone is phenomenal, and DiCaprio is perhaps at his best. Subtle, sinister, and moving. Scorsese's latest masterpiece, and perhaps his best film, completely realising the core themes nearly all of his films have explored, and delivering it in its most human form.

​

**Spectre** and **No Time to Die - 3 and 4/10**

How did we go from the grounded and complex Craig debut of Casino Royale - a film that essentially reinvented the character for our era - into whatever the hell these final two films were? A total retrograde of franchise evolution where characters act without well-developed motivation, the villains are characterless and boring, and the plots are a cut and dry end-of-world conspiracy.  

​

**Contagion - 8/10**

Hindsight is 20/20 (literally in this case) and so watching this film for the first time in 2023, knowing that it was made 8-9 years before covid, is sort of an incredible experience, if not quite a triggering one. It's all a bit clinical and procedural in the way Soderbergh likes to do it, but the moving ending with Damon and his daughter is a beautiful way to return to the human element of these global crises.
